title: predictive-queue-balancer-autoscaler-prd-draft
body:
Summary:

This PRD proposes the Predictive Queue Balancer (PQB) — a hybrid autoscaling and isolation mechanism for Dedicated capacity that smooths tenant microbursts, reduces tail latency, and enforces soft isolation without heavy pre-provisioning. PQB combines short-horizon demand prediction, per-tenant queue buffers, a micro-credit burst allowance, and a small opportunistic pool to maintain service availability and predictable economics.

Why this is needed (background & problem):
- Customers on Dedicated tell us two recurring pain points: (1) sudden microbursts from product spikes degrade latency for other tenants on the same pool, and (2) static reserved capacity or large warm pools are expensive.
- Existing levers (strict quota throttles, binary preemption) are too coarse: they either prevent useful short bursts or cause disruptive evictions.
- Ops needs a principled mechanism that: handles transient excess demand, surfaces predictability guarantees, and keeps unit costs under control.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Reduce P95 generation latency degradation for noisy neighbors by 40% in mixed-tenant pools under realistic mixed workloads.
- Limit evictions/preemptions due to burst overload by 60% versus current soft-preemption policy.
- Ensure predictable billing: burst consumption should be metered separately and visible in Console.
- Provide tenant-level knobs to tune aggressiveness (latency-first vs cost-first) and a safe default.

Non-goals:
- Replace dedicated reservation model. PQB augments dedicated pools; it does not change contract billing.
- Solve for extremely long tail CPU/GPU spikes (minutes+); PQB targets microburst windows (seconds to ~2 minutes).

Key concepts / UX:
1) Queue buffers: each tenant is assigned a lightweight logical queue in front of the serving fabric. Requests can be admitted to the queue and paced into the runtime according to dynamic rates. Queues do not persist long-lived state beyond short-term KV cache pointers.

2) Predictive admission: a tiny on-host predictor uses recent arrival rates and LRU-style pattern detection to estimate short-window demand (5–30s). The predictor increases admission rate proactively when it anticipates a short spike, reducing tokenization/latency penalties from cold scaling.

3) Micro-credit bank (burst allowance): each tenant accrues microcredits proportional to committed capacity and historical steady-state usage. Credits allow short bursts above reserved throughput. Credits decay on a configurable half-life. Consumption appears in billing as a burst usage line item.

4) Opportunistic pool & soft-walled garden: a small pool of opportunistic capacity is available for overflow. Tenants in walled-garden mode are prevented from starving others: when the opportunistic pool is exhausted, PQB gracefully degrades by coalescing short requests (compression windows) or by circuit-breaking from the oldest queued requests rather than wholesale preemption.

5) Fairness & shaping: PQB supports proportional shaping weights to ensure tenant SLOs are respected. We expose per-tenant shape weight and burst policy in the Console config for Dedicated.

System design (high level):
- Admission controller: per-tenant admission agents run colocated with serving nodes. Agents maintain queue head metrics, short-window arrival histograms, and micro-credit counters.
- Central coordinator: lightweight controller (k8s operator) reconciles desired weights, aggregates forecasts across nodes, and nudges opportunistic pool sizing. It also publishes telemetry for Console.
- Runtime integration: PQB inserts at the API gateway -> router layer before kernel scheduling. Admission decisions convert to token claims against the GPU runtime.

Config surface & API changes:
- New route-level fields (in Dedicated route spec):
  - pqb.enabled: boolean
  - pqb.mode: [latency_first | cost_first | balanced]
  - pqb.burst_budget: absolute tokens/second or percentage of committed capacity
  - pqb.credit_decay_seconds: integer
  - pqb.shape_weight: float (0.0-1.0)

- Admin API endpoints (operator):
  - GET /pqb/status (per-pool, per-tenant)
  - POST /pqb/adjust (manual temporary overrides for incidents)

Telemetry & observability:
- New telemetry metrics: queue_length_per_tenant, admission_rate, predictive_confidence (0-1), credit_balance, opportunistic_pool_utilization, evictions_prevented_by_pqb.
- Console: per-route PQB dashboard showing burst usage, credit balance trends, and an alert rule template for sustained opportunistic pool saturation.

SLOs & safety targets:
- Default PQB policy must keep P99 latency regression <= +10% for tenant's own SLO compared to no-interference baseline.
- Opportunistic pool saturation state must raise a critical alert before > 10% of active requests are circuit-broken.

Cost model and billing:
- Burst consumption billed as 'burst tokens' per tenant. Owners can cap monthly burst spend via billing guardrails.
- PQB aims to reduce gross CPU/GPU hours used by avoiding large warm pools; we expect net cost neutral or slightly positive for heavy-burst tenants but lower overall cost for mixed-tenancy customers.

Rollout plan (phases):
Phase 0 — Research & Lab (2 months):
- Build predictor POC using trace replay on representative tenants.
- Simulated experiments for credit accrual math and half-life tuning.

Phase 1 — Canary (1 month):
- Enable PQB in a small dedicated pool with opt-in customers and internal staging workloads. Monitor latency, credit consumption, and opportunistic pool behavior.

Phase 2 — Gradual rollout (2 months):
- Expand to more pools. Enable Console visualization. Expose default config and keep PQB opt-out for customers.

Phase 3 — Default-on beta (3 months):
- After tuning, enable PQB as default for new Dedicated pools with conservative defaults. Offer migration guidance for customers to tune policies.

Operational runbooks (high level):
- If opportunistic pool frequently saturates: increase pool size in controller (short-term), analyze top consumers and consider per-tenant caps.
- If predictive_confidence is low and cold-scaling penalties persist: increase predictor training window or allow slightly higher pre-warm thresholds.
- If microcredit exhaustion spikes quickly: inspect request size distributions and recommend customers adjust pqb.burst_budget or purchase additional committed capacity.

Open questions / risks:
- Predictor safety: how to avoid over-optimistic predictions leading to harmful over-provisioning. Mitigation: conservative confidence threshold and running in passive mode for a baseline period.
- Chargeback UX: customers may be surprised by burst billing unless Console clearly separates committed vs burst usage.
- Multi-region edge cases: PQB coordinator must not create cross-region routing that breaks data residency. Limit PQB decisions to pool-local scope.

Experiment ideas & early metrics to capture:
- A/B test: latency-first vs cost-first modes on similar tenant cohorts and measure P95/P99, CPU/GPU hours, and bake rate of preemptions.
- PTO (play-the-operator): run PQB in a closed test pool and intentionally drive short spikes to measure credit decay and circuit-break frequency.

Appendix (example credit math):
- Credit accrual: credits_per_min = floor(committed_qps * 0.05) + historical_baseline_factor
- Credit half-life: default 30 minutes (configurable per-tenant)
- Example: committed_qps=100, steady_usage=80 -> accrual ~5 credits/minute; 300 credits allow a 100qps burst for ~3 minutes before depleting.

Notes to reviewers (quick):
- Focus review on operational complexity tradeoffs vs expected customer benefit. We intentionally target short spikes (seconds->2min) — longer sustained excess should still be handled by commits.
- Look for integration edges with rollback/fallback policies in the router and Console UX for visibility.

Last updated by Aisha (product) 2026-02-10.
